title: Physiology as Language: Translating Respiration to EEG during Sleep
claim: Condition a masked token-prediction transformer on one signal's embeddings to generate discrete tokens of another modality, decoded back to a continuous signal.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right flow, training/inference branch at right
description: A single wide left-to-right pipeline. At top left, a breathing waveform passes through a trapezoid 'Linear projection' block to produce a column of light-blue Breathing Tokens. Below, a grid of discrete EEG tokens, partly covered by gray 'M' mask cells (partially masked in training, fully masked at inference), maps to a column of EEG Tokens. Both token columns are merged by a bracket into a central green rounded box labeled 'Cross-Modal Transformer'. Its output is a column of Predicted EEG Tokens, shown as a blue-shaded grid. The flow then splits. The Training branch goes to a Cross-Entropy Loss, compared against a Ground-Truth Tokens grid. The Inference branch goes through a blue trapezoid Decoder to a colorful Synthesized EEG spectrogram, with a red-yellow-blue heatmap. The blue token shades and the green transformer box draw the eye first.
caption: Model Pipeline. The model synthesizes sleep EEG from nocturnal breathing signals using an asymmetric embedding strategy
abstract: This paper introduces a novel cross-physiology translation task: synthesizing sleep electroencephalography (EEG) from respiration signals. To address the significant complexity gap between the two modalities, we propose a waveform-conditional generative framework that preserves fine-grained respiratory dynamics while constraining the EEG target space through discrete tokenization. Trained on over 28,000 individuals, our model achieves a 7% Mean Absolute Error in EEG spectrogram reconstruction. Beyond reconstruction, the synthesized EEG supports downstream tasks with performance comparable to ground truth EEG on age estimation (MAE 5.0 vs. 5.1 years), sex detection (AUROC 0.81 vs. 0.82), and sleep staging (Accuracy 0.84 vs. 0.88), significantly outperforming baselines trained directly on breathing. Finally, we demonstrate that the framework generalizes to contactless sensing by synthesizing EEG from wireless radio-frequency reflections, highlighting the feasibility of remote, non-contact neurological assessment during sleep.
